q-tn-modal.label: Verb form after a modal or auxiliary
q-tn-modal.summary: After will, can, may, must, should and similar, the verb is the bare base form, even when other words come in between.

q-tn-subjunctive.label: Verb after demand, insist, suggest
q-tn-subjunctive.summary: After demand, insist, suggest, recommend, request + that, use the base verb, with no -s and no tense.

q-tn-stative.label: Verbs that cannot take -ing
q-tn-stative.summary: Verbs of perception, mental state, feeling and possession (know, believe, want, own, have=possess, resemble, seem) describe a state and never take the continuous form.

q-tn-sincefor.label: 'Since' a point, 'for' a length
q-tn-sincefor.summary: 'Since' names the point a period began (since 2019, since Monday) and pairs with a simple-past clause; 'for' names the period's length (for two years) and never follows 'since'.

q-tn-definite.label: Present perfect with a named past time
q-tn-definite.summary: The moment a sentence names a finished point in time (yesterday, last year, in 2016, two days ago), the verb must be simple past, not present perfect.

q-tn-sequence.label: Past perfect / future perfect for the earlier action
q-tn-sequence.summary: Of two past actions, the earlier one takes the past perfect (before/after/by the time/found that); when the same signpost points at the future, the later action takes the future perfect.

q-tn-itstime.label: 'It's time' + simple past, not a modal
q-tn-itstime.summary: 'It is (high) time' is followed by a subject and the simple past, or by 'to' and the base verb with no subject — never by a modal such as 'should'.

rules.text: After a modal (will, would, can, could, may, might, shall, should, must) the verb is the bare base form: no -s, no -ed, no -ing, no to. Words placed between the modal and the verb (such as 'without any pressure') do not change this.
rules.ok: Regional bodies will, without any pressure, comply.
rules.bad: Regional bodies will, without any pressure, complies.

rules.text: After demand, insist, suggest, recommend, request, propose, order + that, the verb is the base form (subjunctive) whatever the subject. 'Demand' cannot take 'me to': say 'demanded that I ...'.
rules.ok: She demanded that I swallow the medication.
rules.bad: She demanded me to swallow the medication.

rules.text: Verbs of perception, mental state, feeling, or possession (see, hear, know, think, believe, want, like, love, hate, own, have meaning possess, belong, resemble, seem, appear, remember, mean) describe a state rather than an ongoing action, so they do not take -ing even in a sentence that feels like 'right now'. 'Have' keeps this rule only when it means possess; when it names an action (have breakfast, have a bath, have a look) it can take -ing.
rules.ok: He owns three shops in that market.
rules.bad: He is owning three shops in that market.

rules.text: 'Since' names the point at which an unbroken period began (since 2008, since Monday, since morning); 'for' names the period's length (for two years, for a week) and never follows 'since'. A clause that opens with 'since' is in the simple past; the clause it supports is in the present perfect (or past perfect, if the whole sentence is already set in the past).
rules.ok: I have not met him since he left the city.
rules.bad: I have not met him since twenty years.

rules.text: The present perfect reports an action with no stated point in past time, or one still connected to the present. The instant a sentence names a finished point in the past — yesterday, last year, in 1998, two days ago, 'when' + simple past — the verb must switch to simple past.
rules.bad: She has submitted the report yesterday.

rules.text: When a sentence reports two past actions, the one that happened first takes the past perfect and the one that happened second takes the simple past, usually signalled by 'before', 'after', 'by the time', or '...found that...'. When the same 'by the time' signpost points at the future instead, the later action takes the future perfect, not the simple future.
rules.ok: By the time the manager arrived, the workers had already left.
rules.bad: By the time the manager arrived, the workers already left.

rules.text: 'It is (high) time' is followed by a subject and the simple past — not a modal such as 'should' — to say something is overdue, or by 'to' and the base verb with the subject left out.
rules.ok: It is time you left for the station.
rules.bad: It is time you should leave for the station.

q-tn-modal.cue: A long sentence with 'will', 'can' or 'must' and a verb that appears several words later.
q-tn-modal.standard: Find the modal in each part and join it to the verb that belongs with it, skipping the words in between. The verb must be in its base form.
q-tn-modal.fast: Look for -s / -ed / -ing verbs after a modal.
q-tn-modal.eliminate: Parts without a verb cannot hold the error; skip them.
traps: A plural subject far from the verb making you read 'comply'; the real fault is the -s.
Words between the modal and the verb hide the mismatch.

q-tn-subjunctive.cue: demanded / insisted / suggested / recommended + a person + 'to' or 'that' and a verb.
q-tn-subjunctive.standard: Replace 'demand + me to' with 'demand that I' and put the verb in the base form.
q-tn-subjunctive.fast: Pick the option with 'that' + base verb.
q-tn-subjunctive.eliminate: Drop options that use 'me to' or 'by me', or put an object pronoun ('that me') in the subject slot.
traps: 'Demanded me to' copies the pattern of 'asked me to', which works for ask but not demand.
'That me' puts an object pronoun in the subject position.

q-tn-stative.cue: A verb of knowing, owning, believing, wanting or seeming ending in -ing.
q-tn-stative.standard: Replace the -ing form with the plain present (or past) and check the sentence still reports a state, not an action.
q-tn-stative.eliminate: Keep an -ing option only if the verb is 'have' used for an action (have lunch, have a look), not possession.
traps: 'Is having' meaning possess copies the pattern of 'is having lunch', which is the one case where -ing is fine.
A sentence that 'feels' continuous (he is owning...) still fails if the verb is stative.

q-tn-sincefor.cue: 'since' followed by a number of days/months/years, or a duration phrase after 'since'.
q-tn-sincefor.standard: Check what follows 'since': it must be a point (a year, a day, an event), never a length. A length needs 'for'.
q-tn-sincefor.fast: 'since' + a bare number of units (since twenty years, since centuries) is always wrong; it should be 'for'.
q-tn-sincefor.eliminate: Rule out any option that keeps 'since' in front of a duration.
traps: 'Since' sounds natural before any time word, but it only takes a starting point, never a span.
The verb tense in the since-clause (simple past) is a separate, equally tested fault.

q-tn-definite.cue: A present-perfect verb (has/have + V3) next to yesterday, last year, ago, or a specific date.
q-tn-definite.standard: If a finished point in past time is named anywhere in the clause, change has/have + V3 to the simple past.
q-tn-definite.fast: has/have + V3 + yesterday/ago/last ___/in [year] is always wrong.
q-tn-definite.eliminate: An option that keeps 'has/have' when a date or 'ago' is present cannot be right.
traps: The action feels recent, so present perfect looks natural, but a named date overrides that feeling.
'Last' and 'ago' are the two words most often missed while scanning.

q-tn-sequence.cue: Two past actions in one sentence, joined by before/after/by the time/when, both in the simple past (or both in a future form).
q-tn-sequence.standard: Decide which action happened first. Put the earlier one in the past perfect (or future perfect, if the sentence is about the future) and leave the later one as it is.
q-tn-sequence.fast: before/after/by the time + two same-tense verbs is a signal one of them should be perfect.
q-tn-sequence.eliminate: Rule out any option that leaves both verbs in the simple past (or simple future) when the sentence clearly reports which came first.
traps: Both verbs being in the same tense feels balanced, but exactly one of them needs to mark 'already done by then'.
'By the time' pointing at the future is often misread as needing the simple future for both verbs.

q-tn-itstime.cue: 'It is time' or 'it is high time' followed by a subject and a modal such as 'should'.
q-tn-itstime.standard: Drop the modal: 'it is time' + subject takes the simple past directly, or rephrase with 'to' + base verb and no subject.
q-tn-itstime.fast: 'it's (high) time' + subject + should + V1 is always wrong.
q-tn-itstime.eliminate: Rule out any option that keeps 'should' after 'it's time' with a named subject.
traps: 'Should' feels like the natural modal for an overdue action, but this fixed idiom does not take one.

pyqs.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
That the policy omits provisions for backward compatibility / is less troubling than the belief / that all regional bodies will, without any pressure, / complies with the central directive as issued.
options: That the policy omits provisions for backward compatibility
is less troubling than the belief
that all regional bodies will, without any pressure,
complies with the central directive as issued.
pyqs.why: 'Will' needs a base verb, so 'complies' must be 'comply'. The phrase 'without any pressure' sits between them and hides the pair.

a.note: A 'That' clause subject with 'omits': the verb agrees with 'policy', so it is correct.

b.note: 'Is less troubling than the belief' is a correct singular verb phrase for the clause subject.

c.note: 'All regional bodies will' correctly starts the pair; the fault is in the verb that completes it.

pyqs.text:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:
She [[demanded me to swallow the medication]].
options: demanded that I swallow the medication
to swallow the medication by me
pyqs.why: 'Demand' takes a that-clause with the base verb: 'demanded that I swallow'. It cannot be followed by 'me to'.

b.note: 'Demanded me swallowing' is not a correct pattern.

c.note: 'That me swallow' puts the object form 'me' where the subject 'I' is needed.

d.note: 'By me' is a passive-style ending that does not fit 'demanded'.

practice.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
The firm said that / it can, if the weather permits, / completes the work / before the festival.
options: it can, if the weather permits,
practice.why: 'Can' needs the base verb, so 'completes' must be 'complete'; the if-clause sits between them.

a.note: Reporting verb in the past; there is no error.

b.note: 'It can' is correct and starts the pair.

d.note: 'Before the festival' is a correct phrase of time.

practice.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
Nobody believed that / the old bridge could, despite the repairs, / to bear the weight / of the heavy trucks.
options: the old bridge could, despite the repairs,
practice.why: After 'could' the verb is bare: 'bear', not 'to bear'.

b.note: 'Could' starts the pair and is correct.

d.note: A correct 'of' phrase.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The committee recommended that the rule ___ revised at once.
practice.why: After 'recommend that' the base form is used, so the passive becomes 'be revised'.

a.note: The ordinary present is used here, but 'recommended that' needs the base verb.

c.note: A past form is used here, but the verb after 'recommend that' is the base form.

d.note: The present perfect is used here instead of the base form that 'recommended that' requires.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The coach insisted that every player ___ at six sharp.
practice.why: After 'insisted that' the base verb is used for every subject: 'arrive'.

a.note: The -s form agrees with 'every player' in the ordinary way, but this verb needs the base form.

c.note: A past form is used here, but 'insist that' takes the base verb.

d.note: An -ing form cannot be the finite verb of the clause.

practice.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
The principal announced that / the students should, before the examination begins, / submits their forms / to the clerk.
options: the students should, before the examination begins,
practice.why: 'Should' needs the bare verb, so 'submits' must be 'submit'. The clause 'before the examination begins' separates the modal from its verb.

a.note: A reporting clause in the past; there is no error in it.

b.note: 'The students should' correctly begins the modal pair.

d.note: 'To the clerk' is a prepositional phrase with no verb.

practice.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
Everybody knows that / a careful driver will never, / whatever the hurry, / crosses a red light.
practice.why: 'Will' takes the bare verb, so 'crosses' must be 'cross'; the phrase 'whatever the hurry' hides the pair.

a.note: 'Everybody knows that' is correct, with a singular verb for 'everybody'.

b.note: 'A careful driver will never' correctly begins the modal pair.

c.note: 'Whatever the hurry' is a phrase with no finite verb.

practice.text:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:
The manager [[suggested him to revise the estimate]].
options: suggested that he revise the estimate
suggested that he revises the estimate
suggested to him revise the estimate
practice.why: 'Suggest' cannot take 'him to'; it takes a that-clause with the base verb: suggested that he revise.

b.note: 'Suggested him revising' is not a pattern 'suggest' allows.

c.note: The that-clause is right, but after 'suggest that' the verb stays in the base form, so 'revises' is wrong.

d.note: 'Suggested to him revise' leaves the clause without 'that' and the verb without a subject.

practice.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
The old caretaker / is knowing every family / in this locality / for forty years.
practice.why: 'Know' is a stative verb and never takes the continuous form: it should be 'has known'.

a.note: A plain subject phrase; no verb to fault here.

c.note: A prepositional phrase of place.

d.note: 'For forty years' is a correct duration phrase once the verb itself is fixed.

practice.text:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:
She said she [[is not meaning]] to upset anyone by her remark.
practice.why: 'Mean' is stative; it never takes -ing. In reported past speech the plain past, 'did not mean', is what the sentence needs.

b.note: 'Is not meant' turns the verb passive, which is not what the sentence is saying.

c.note: Still keeps the -ing form on a stative verb, only shifting it to the past continuous.

d.note: 'Has not meant' does not fit a speech reported in the simple past.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
This old house ___ to my grandfather, not to the bank.
practice.why: 'Belong' is a stative verb of possession; it is never used in the continuous form.

a.note: Puts the stative verb 'belong' into the continuous, which it cannot take.

c.note: Not a standard English form.

d.note: A passive continuous is not possible with 'belong'.

practice.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
Although he is having / a large collection of old coins, / he rarely shows it / to visitors.
options: a large collection of old coins,
practice.why: 'Have' meaning possess cannot take -ing: it should be 'Although he has a large collection'.

b.note: A correct noun phrase, the object of 'have'.

c.note: Correct once the first part is fixed.

d.note: A correct prepositional phrase.

practice.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
The two villages / have been disputing over the land / since nearly thirty years / without any settlement.
options: have been disputing over the land
practice.why: 'Since' can only name a starting point, never a length of time; 'nearly thirty years' is a duration, so it needs 'for'.

b.note: A correct present perfect continuous for an unfinished dispute.

d.note: A correct closing phrase.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
He has not touched a drop of alcohol ___ his heart surgery two years ago.
practice.why: The surgery is a fixed point in the past, so the sentence needs 'since', not a duration word.

a.note: 'For' names a length, but 'his heart surgery' is a point in time, not a span.

c.note: 'From' does not pair with 'has not touched' in this sense.

d.note: 'During' needs an ongoing period, not a single past event.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
Nobody has visited this old office ___ many months.
practice.why: 'Many months' is a span of time (a duration), so it takes 'for'; 'since' only takes a starting point such as a date or an event.

b.note: 'Since' only pairs with a starting point (since 2008, since Monday), never with a plain span like 'many months'.

c.note: 'During' needs a defined period introduced by 'the' (during the past months), not a bare span.

d.note: 'Within' points to a deadline not yet reached, which does not fit a present-perfect sentence about time already elapsed.

practice.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
I have been waiting / for this reply / since last three weeks, / and still nothing has come.
practice.why: 'Last three weeks' is a duration, not a point, so it must follow 'for', not 'since'.

d.note: A correct closing clause.

practice.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
The committee / has submitted its final report / to the ministry / last Friday.
practice.why: 'Last Friday' names a finished point in the past, so the verb must be simple past: 'submitted', not 'has submitted'.

c.note: A correct prepositional phrase.

d.note: A correct time phrase, which is exactly why the verb before it must change.

practice.text:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:
She [[has joined this college in 2019]] and has not missed a single class since.
practice.why: 'In 2019' is a dated point in the past, so the simple past 'joined' is needed, not the present perfect.

b.note: Changing 'in' to 'since' does not fix the real fault, which is the verb tense before a dated year.

c.note: The present continuous does not fit a completed joining in a past year.

d.note: The past perfect wrongly implies this joining happened before some other past event, which the sentence never mentions.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The results ___ out two days ago, yet nobody has checked the portal.
practice.why: 'Two days ago' is a finished point in the past, so the verb must be simple past: 'came'.

a.note: Present perfect does not combine with a named 'ago' phrase.

c.note: Same fault, plus a subject-verb mismatch with the plural 'results'.

d.note: The present continuous does not fit a completed, dated event.

practice.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
I have finished / reading that novel / in the summer / of last year.
practice.why: 'In the summer of last year' is a dated past period, so the verb must be simple past: 'I finished'.

c.note: A correct phrase of time, which is exactly why the verb before it must change.

d.note: Completes the time phrase correctly.

practice.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
By the time / the ambulance reached the spot, / the injured man already died / of his wounds.
practice.why: The man's death happened before the ambulance's arrival, so it needs the past perfect: 'had already died'.

a.note: A correct signal phrase for sequence.

b.note: A correct simple past for the later action.

d.note: A correct closing phrase.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
Before the teacher could stop him, the boy ___ out of the room.
practice.why: The boy's exit happened before the teacher's (failed) attempt to stop him, so the earlier action needs the past perfect: 'had run'.

a.note: Simple present does not fit a past narrative.

b.note: Simple past matches the later action's tense but does not mark that this action came first.

d.note: Present perfect does not fit a sentence already set in the past.

practice.text:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:
By the time the auditors [[arrive]], the staff will have cleared every pending file.
practice.why: With 'by the time' pointing at the future and the main clause already in the future perfect, the time clause stays in the simple present: 'arrive'.

b.note: A simple past would set the whole sentence in the past, clashing with 'will have cleared'.

c.note: Two future forms in one 'by the time' sentence is the classic error this construction tests; only one clause should carry 'will'.

d.note: Present perfect does not fit a 'by the time' clause pointing at the future.

practice.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
When the fire brigade / arrived at the warehouse, / the flames already spread / to the next building.
practice.why: The spreading happened before the brigade's arrival, so it needs the past perfect: 'had already spread'.

b.note: A correct simple past for the later action.

d.note: A correct closing phrase.

practice.text:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:
It is high time [[that the government should take]] strict action against such offenders.
practice.why: 'It is high time' is followed by a subject and the simple past, not a modal: 'the government took'.

b.note: The simple present does not fit the idiom 'it's (high) time'.

c.note: Swaps one modal, 'should', for another, 'would'; the idiom still takes no modal at all.

d.note: 'Will' is a modal pointing to the future, which this idiom about an overdue action does not take.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
It's time the committee ___ a final decision on the matter.
practice.why: 'It's time' + subject takes the simple past: 'made'.

a.note: The simple present does not fit this fixed idiom.

c.note: No modal follows 'it's time' when a subject is named.

d.note: 'Will' points to the future, which clashes with the idiom's sense of 'overdue now'.

practice.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
It is time / we should stop / blaming each other / and start fixing the problem.
practice.why: After 'it is time' + a named subject, the verb is the simple past with no modal: 'we stopped', not 'we should stop'.

a.note: The idiom itself is correctly formed.

c.note: A correct non-finite phrase, the object of 'stop'.

d.note: A correct closing phrase.
